sections.title: HADOOP — Data Ingestion: create an HDFS directory and transfer bank.csv
sections.answer: A single-node Hadoop cluster (NameNode, DataNode, ResourceManager, NodeManager) was started with ./start_cluster.sh. The directory /user/<user>/banking/input was created in HDFS and bank.csv copied into it. The file is stored with a 128 KB block size so HDFS splits it into 3 blocks — like real big data — which later gives every MapReduce job 3 parallel map tasks.

sections.title: Data Analysis with MapReduce — relationship between age and balance (summarised)
sections.answer: Mapper puts every client into a 10-year age band; the reducer reports count, min, average, median and max balance per band. Findings: average balance rises steadily with age up to 70-79 (3,280.87) and then falls; medians are far below averages in every band, so a few very rich clients pull the averages up; negative balances (overdrafts) appear only below age 70.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Job 5 mapper: put each client in a 10-year age band and emit  band \t balance"""
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from common import parse

for line in sys.stdin:
    row = parse(line)
    if row:
        age = int(row["age"])
        low = (age // 10) * 10
        print(f"{low:02d}-{low + 9}\t{row['balance']}")

# ---- job5_reducer.py ----
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Job 5 reducer: for each age band print count, min, avg, median and max balance."""
import sys
from statistics import median

current, values = None, []

def flush():
    if current is not None:
        print(f"{current}\t{len(values)}\t{min(values)}\t"
              f"{sum(values) / len(values):.2f}\t{median(values):.1f}\t{max(values)}")

for line in sys.stdin:
    key, value = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    if key != current:
        flush()
        current, values = key, []
    values.append(int(value))
flush()

sections.title: HIVE — Data Ingestion and Table Creation: database banking_data, table client_info, load bank.csv
sections.answer: Hive runs as HiveServer2 (./start_hive.sh) with its warehouse on HDFS. run_hive.sh copies bank.csv inside HDFS without the header line, then the statements below create the database and the typed table and load the data. Numbers are INT, categories STRING; `default` needs back-ticks because it is a reserved word.
sections.code:
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS banking_data
COMMENT 'Bank marketing clients (bank.csv)';
USE banking_data;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS client_info;
CREATE TABLE client_info (
  age INT,
  job STRING,
  marital STRING,
  education STRING,
  `default` STRING,
  balance INT,
  housing STRING,
  loan STRING,
  contact STRING,
  day INT,
  month STRING,
  duration INT,
  campaign INT,
  pdays INT,
  previous INT,
  poutcome STRING,
  y STRING
)
COMMENT 'One row per client contacted in the term-deposit campaign'
ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','
STORED AS TEXTFILE;

-- run_hive.sh copies bank.csv from HDFS input to HDFS staging without its header line, then we load it
LOAD DATA INPATH '/user/${env:USER}/banking/staging/bank.csv' OVERWRITE INTO TABLE client_info;
DESCRIBE client_info;

sections.title: HIVE — Trend Analysis — year-over-year trend in the number of clients contacted
sections.answer: bank.csv has day and month but NO year column, so a true year-over-year trend cannot be computed from this file. The query shows the trend along the time axis the data does have — contacts and success rate per calendar month, with LAG() giving the change versus the previous month. Contacts jump from 293 in April to 1,398 in May (+1,105) and then fall; the success rate moves opposite to volume (6.65% in May vs 42.9% in March and 46.3% in October).
sections.code:
hive> SELECT month_no, month, contacts, success_rate_pct,
    >   contacts - LAG(contacts) OVER (ORDER BY month_no) AS change_vs_prev_month
    > FROM (
    >   SELECT CASE month WHEN 'jan' THEN 1 WHEN 'feb' THEN 2 WHEN 'mar' THEN 3 WHEN 'apr' THEN 4
    >   WHEN 'may' THEN 5 WHEN 'jun' THEN 6 WHEN 'jul' THEN 7 WHEN 'aug' THEN 8
    >   WHEN 'sep' THEN 9 WHEN 'oct' THEN 10 WHEN 'nov' THEN 11 ELSE 12 END AS month_no,
    >   month,
    >   COUNT(*) AS contacts,
    >   ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN y = 'yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS success_rate_pct
    >   FROM client_info GROUP BY month
    > ) m
    > ORDER BY month_no;

sections.title: HIVE — Anomaly Detection — unusual patterns in average yearly balance across education levels
sections.answer: Step 1 shows the spread per education level, step 2 counts outliers (> mean + 3 std) and negative balances. Unusual patterns: primary education has the largest spread (std 3,711) and the single largest balance (71,188) despite a low median; tertiary has the most high outliers (41) and the lowest minimum (-3,313); secondary has the most overdrawn clients (228). In every group the mean is 3-4x the median — balance is heavily right-skewed.
sections.code:
hive> SELECT education, COUNT(*) AS clients,
    >   ROUND(AVG(balance), 2) AS avg_bal,
    >   PERCENTILE(balance, 0.5) AS median_bal,
    >   ROUND(STDDEV_POP(balance), 2) AS std_bal,
    >   MIN(balance) AS min_bal, MAX(balance) AS max_bal
    > FROM client_info GROUP BY education ORDER BY avg_bal DESC;

hive> SELECT c.education,
    >   SUM(IF(c.balance > o.mu + 3 * o.sd, 1, 0)) AS high_outliers,
    >   SUM(IF(c.balance < 0, 1, 0)) AS negative_bal,
    >   ROUND(AVG(c.balance) - MAX(o.mu), 2) AS gap_vs_overall
    > FROM client_info c
    > CROSS JOIN (SELECT AVG(balance) mu, STDDEV_POP(balance) sd FROM client_info) o
    > GROUP BY c.education ORDER BY high_outliers DESC;

docs.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Spark
docs.intro: Apache Spark 4.0.1 (PySpark) in VS Code, local[4] = 4 parallel tasks. Notebook: 02_eda_spark.ipynb (run in VS Code, not Colab).

sections.title: Spark session (setup used by every question)
sections.answer: Spark 4.0.1 runs in local mode with 4 worker threads (local[4]): the DataFrame is split into partitions and each partition is processed by a separate task in parallel — the same code runs unchanged on a cluster.
sections.code:
import os, sys, time
# Spark needs Java 17; point to Homebrew's JDK if JAVA_HOME is not already set
os.environ.setdefault("JAVA_HOME", "/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk@17/libexec/openjdk.jdk/Contents/Home")
os.environ["PYSPARK_PYTHON"] = sys.executable          # workers use this venv's Python
os.environ.setdefault("SPARK_LOCAL_IP", "127.0.0.1")    # single machine: bind to localhost
os.chdir(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath("__file__")) if os.path.exists("data") else "..")

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, types as T

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .appName("Bank-EDA")
         .master("local[4]")                          # 4 worker threads = 4 parallel tasks
         .config("spark.driver.memory", "2g")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")  # small data -> fewer shuffle partitions
         .config("spark.hadoop.fs.defaultFS", "file:///")  # read local files even if HADOOP_CONF_DIR is set
         .config("spark.ui.showConsoleProgress", "false")
         .getOrCreate())
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
DATA = "data/bank.csv"
print("Spark", spark.version, "| master:", spark.sparkContext.master,
      "| default parallelism:", spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism)
print("Spark UI (while this notebook runs): http://localhost:4040")

sections.title: Data Preprocessing — handle missing values
sections.answer: No column has nulls; 'unknown' is kept as a real category (for poutcome it means 'never contacted'). A fill step (median for numbers, 'unknown' for categories) still protects the pipeline from future nulls.
sections.code:
null_counts = df.select([F.sum(F.col(c).isNull().cast("int")).alias(c) for c in df.columns])
null_counts.show()

num_cols = ["age", "balance", "day", "duration", "campaign", "pdays", "previous"]
cat_cols = ["job", "marital", "education", "default", "housing", "loan", "contact", "month", "poutcome"]

# safety net: numeric nulls -> median, categorical nulls -> 'unknown'
medians = dict(zip(num_cols, df.approxQuantile(num_cols, [0.5], 0.01)))
df = df.fillna({c: float(m[0]) for c, m in medians.items()}).fillna("unknown", subset=cat_cols)
print("rows after handling missing values:", df.count())

sections.title: Data Preprocessing — handle outliers
sections.answer: IQR fences from exact quartiles. balance (506 outliers), duration (330) and campaign (318) are capped instead of deleted so no real client is thrown away; pdays/previous are left alone because -1/0 are codes.
sections.code:
cap_cols = ["balance", "duration", "campaign"]
q = df.approxQuantile(cap_cols, [0.25, 0.75], 0.0)       # exact quartiles, computed in parallel
fences = {}
for c, (q1, q3) in zip(cap_cols, q):
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    n_out = df.filter((F.col(c) < lo) | (F.col(c) > hi)).count()
    fences[c] = (lo, hi)
    print(f"{c:9s} Q1={q1:8.1f} Q3={q3:8.1f}  fences=[{lo:9.1f}, {hi:9.1f}]  outliers={n_out}")

for c, (lo, hi) in fences.items():
    df = df.withColumn(c, F.when(F.col(c) < lo, lo).when(F.col(c) > hi, hi).otherwise(F.col(c)).cast("double"))
df.select(cap_cols).describe().show()

from pyspark.ml.classification import (LogisticRegression, DecisionTreeClassifier,
                                       RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier)
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

auc_roc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", rawPredictionCol="probability", metricName="areaUnderROC")
auc_pr  = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", rawPredictionCol="probability", metricName="areaUnderPR")

def scores(pred, threshold=0.5):
    """All metrics from one distributed pass: AUCs + confusion matrix for the positive class."""
    p1 = F.udf(lambda v: float(v[1]), T.DoubleType())
    pred = pred.withColumn("p_yes", p1("probability")).withColumn("pred_t", (F.col("p_yes") >= threshold).cast("double"))
    cm = pred.groupBy().agg(
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 1) & (F.col("pred_t") == 1)).cast("int")).alias("tp"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 0) & (F.col("pred_t") == 1)).cast("int")).alias("fp"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 1) & (F.col("pred_t") == 0)).cast("int")).alias("fn"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 0) & (F.col("pred_t") == 0)).cast("int")).alias("tn")).first()
    tp, fp, fn, tn = cm["tp"], cm["fp"], cm["fn"], cm["tn"]
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return {"AUC_ROC": auc_roc.evaluate(pred), "AUC_PR": auc_pr.evaluate(pred),
            "accuracy": (tp + tn) / (tp + tn + fp + fn), "precision_yes": precision,
            "recall_yes": recall, "F1_yes": f1, "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn}

def scores(pred, threshold=0.5):
    """All metrics from one distributed pass: AUCs + confusion matrix for the positive class."""
    p1 = F.udf(lambda v: float(v[1]), T.DoubleType())
    pred = pred.withColumn("p_yes", p1("probability")).withColumn("pred_t", (F.col("p_yes") >= threshold).cast("double"))
    cm = pred.groupBy().agg(
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 1) & (F.col("pred_t") == 1)).cast("int")).alias("tp"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 0) & (F.col("pred_t") == 1)).cast("int")).alias("fp"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 1) & (F.col("pred_t") == 0)).cast("int")).alias("fn"),
        F.sum(((F.col("label") == 0) & (F.col("pred_t") == 0)).cast("int")).alias("tn")).first()
    tp, fp, fn, tn = cm["tp"], cm["fp"], cm["fn"], cm["tn"]
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return {"AUC_ROC": auc_roc.evaluate(pred), "AUC_PR": auc_pr.evaluate(pred),
            "accuracy": (tp + tn) / (tp + tn + fp + fn), "precision_yes": precision,
            "recall_yes": recall, "F1_yes": f1, "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn}

           .addGrid(lr.regParam, [0.0, 0.01, 0.1])
           .addGrid(lr.elasticNetParam, [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])

sections.title: Simulated real-time feed — producer (breaks bank.csv into chunks)
sections.answer: producer.py shuffles bank.csv, cuts it into 29 files of 150 rows and writes one file every 2 seconds into a folder that Spark watches. Each row gets txn_id and event_time (each file = 10 s of event time). To make it realistic, about 5% of rows are late / out-of-order (15-90 s old) and one file is a 3x traffic burst. Files are written to a temp name and renamed so Spark never reads half a file.
sections.code:
ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--chunk-size", type=int, default=150)
    ap.add_argument("--interval", type=float, default=2.0, help="seconds between files")
    ap.add_argument("--late-fraction", type=float, default=0.05)
    ap.add_argument("--burst-chunk", type=int, default=12)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=os.path.join(ROOT, "04_streaming", "stream_input"))
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=7)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    random.seed(args.seed)
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "bank.csv"))))
    random.shuffle(rows)                       # mix clients so every chunk looks like live traffic
    os.makedirs(args.out, exist_ok=True)
    fields = ["txn_id", "event_time"] + list(rows[0].keys())

    now = datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)
    base = now - timedelta(seconds=now.second % 10)      # align to 10 s so each chunk = one 10 s window
    pos, chunk, txn, late_total = 0, 0, 0, 0
    while pos < len(rows):
        size = args.chunk_size * (3 if chunk == args.burst_chunk else 1)
        part = rows[pos:pos + size]
        pos += size
        start = base + timedelta(seconds=10 * chunk)
        out_rows = []
        for r in part:
            txn += 1
            et = start + timedelta(seconds=random.uniform(0, 10))
            if random.random() < args.late_fraction:          # late + out-of-order event
                et -= timedelta(seconds=random.uniform(15, 90))
                late_total += 1
            out_rows.append({"txn_id": txn, "event_time": et.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), **r})
        random.shuffle(out_rows)                               # out-of-order inside the file too
        tmp = os.path.join(args.out, f".chunk_{chunk:03d}.tmp")
        with open(tmp, "w", newline="") as f:
            w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
            w.writeheader()
            w.writerows(out_rows)
        os.rename(tmp, os.path.join(args.out, f"chunk_{chunk:03d}.csv"))   # atomic: Spark never sees half a file
        tag = "  <- BURST (3x traffic)" if chunk == args.burst_chunk else ""
        print(f"[producer] chunk {chunk:02d}: {len(out_rows):3d} rows, event time "
              f"{start.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}-{(start + timedelta(seconds=10)).strftime('%H:%M:%S')}{tag}", flush=True)
        chunk += 1
        time.sleep(args.interval)
    print(f"[producer] done: {txn} transactions in {chunk} files, {late_total} late/out-of-order", flush=True)

sections.title: 1. Stream Processing and Data Aggregation — average balance and duration per job, in real time
sections.answer: Spark Structured Streaming (the current streaming API in Spark 4) reads the folder as a stream with an explicit schema. groupBy(job) keeps a running count, average balance and average duration; complete mode re-emits the table after every micro-batch. After the last batch the numbers equal the batch Hadoop/Hive results exactly (e.g. management 1,766.93, retired 2,319.19) — streaming and batch agree.
sections.code:
def read_stream(spark):
    # File source: every new CSV dropped in STREAM_DIR becomes part of the next micro-batch.
    # A streaming source needs an explicit schema (Spark cannot scan an unbounded folder to infer it).
    return (spark.readStream.schema(SCHEMA).option("header", True)
            .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1)          # 1 file per micro-batch -> visible, steady flow
            .csv(STREAM_DIR))


def part1(spark, stream):
    banner("PART 1 - Real-time aggregation: average balance and call duration per job (updated every batch)")
    agg = (stream.groupBy("job")
           .agg(F.count("*").alias("transactions"),
                F.round(F.avg("balance"), 2).alias("avg_balance"),
                F.round(F.avg("duration"), 1).alias("avg_duration_sec")))

    def show(batch_df, batch_id):
        if batch_df.isEmpty():
            return
        total = batch_df.agg(F.sum("transactions")).first()[0]
        print(f"\n----- micro-batch {batch_id}: running totals after {total} transactions -----", flush=True)
        batch_df.orderBy(F.desc("transactions")).show(15, truncate=False)
        batch_df.toPandas().to_csv(os.path.join(RESULTS, "part1_job_aggregates_latest.csv"), index=False)

    # complete mode = the whole (small) result table is re-emitted every batch
    return [agg.writeStream.outputMode("complete").foreachBatch(show)
            .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p1").trigger(processingTime="2 seconds").start()]

sections.title: 2. Real-Time Model Predictions — trained model integrated into the stream
sections.answer: The model is the tuned Logistic Regression pipeline trained on the historical bank.csv in Part 3 (if it is missing, the app trains one on the CSV first). The same outlier caps are applied, and every incoming transaction gets 'predicted' (yes/no) and p_subscribe. Each batch prints its most promising leads and running metrics. After all 4,521 transactions: accuracy 82.9%, recall (yes) 82.0%, precision (yes) 38.5%. (The stream replays bank.csv, so most rows were also training rows; the Part 3 test set is the unbiased estimate.)
sections.code:
def load_or_train_model(spark):
    """Use the tuned pipeline from Part 3; if it is missing, train a quick one on the historical CSV."""
    from pyspark.ml import PipelineModel
    path = os.path.join(ROOT, "models", "term_deposit_best")
    meta = os.path.join(ROOT, "models", "preprocessing.json")
    if os.path.exists(path) and os.path.exists(meta):
        info = json.load(open(meta))
        print(f"loaded model from Part 3: {info['model']}  (models/term_deposit_best)", flush=True)
        return PipelineModel.load(path), info["cap_fences"]

    print("Part 3 model not found -> training a Logistic Regression on data/bank.csv", flush=True)
    from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
    from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
    from pyspark.ml.feature import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler, StringIndexer, VectorAssembler
    cats = ["job", "marital", "education", "default", "housing", "loan", "contact", "month", "poutcome"]
    nums = ["age", "balance", "day", "duration", "campaign", "pdays", "previous", "was_contacted_before"]
    hist = (spark.read.csv(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "bank.csv"), header=True, inferSchema=True)
            .withColumn("was_contacted_before", (F.col("pdays") != -1).cast("double"))
            .withColumn("label", (F.col("y") == "yes").cast("double")))
    pipe = Pipeline(stages=[*[StringIndexer(inputCol=c, outputCol=c + "_idx", handleInvalid="keep") for c in cats],
                            OneHotEncoder(inputCols=[c + "_idx" for c in cats], outputCols=[c + "_ohe" for c in cats]),
                            VectorAssembler(inputCols=nums + [c + "_ohe" for c in cats], outputCol="raw_features"),
                            StandardScaler(inputCol="raw_features", outputCol="features"),
                            LogisticRegression(labelCol="label", regParam=0.01)])
    return pipe.fit(hist), {}


def part2(spark, stream):
    banner("PART 2 - Real-time model predictions: every incoming transaction gets a subscribe/no prediction")
    model, fences = load_or_train_model(spark)
    feats = stream.withColumn("was_contacted_before", (F.col("pdays") != -1).cast("double"))
    for c, (lo, hi) in fences.items():           # same outlier caps as training
        feats = feats.withColumn(c, F.least(F.greatest(F.col(c).cast("double"), F.lit(lo)), F.lit(hi)))
    p_yes = F.udf(lambda v: float(v[1]), T.DoubleType())
    scored = (model.transform(feats)
              .withColumn("p_subscribe", F.round(p_yes("probability"), 3))
              .withColumn("predicted", F.when(F.col("prediction") == 1, "yes").otherwise("no"))
              .select("txn_id", "event_time", "age", "job", "balance", "duration", "y", "predicted", "p_subscribe"))

    totals = {"n": 0, "correct": 0, "tp": 0, "fp": 0, "fn": 0}

    def show(batch_df, batch_id):
        if batch_df.isEmpty():
            return
        batch_df = batch_df.cache()
        m = batch_df.agg(F.count("*").alias("n"),
                         F.sum((F.col("y") == F.col("predicted")).cast("int")).alias("correct"),
                         F.sum(((F.col("y") == "yes") & (F.col("predicted") == "yes")).cast("int")).alias("tp"),
                         F.sum(((F.col("y") == "no") & (F.col("predicted") == "yes")).cast("int")).alias("fp"),
                         F.sum(((F.col("y") == "yes") & (F.col("predicted") == "no")).cast("int")).alias("fn")).first()
        for k in totals:
            totals[k] += m[k]
        rec = totals["tp"] / max(totals["tp"] + totals["fn"], 1)
        prec = totals["tp"] / max(totals["tp"] + totals["fp"], 1)
        print(f"\n----- micro-batch {batch_id}: {m['n']} new transactions scored | batch accuracy "
              f"{m['correct'] / m['n']:.1%} | running: {totals['n']} scored, accuracy "
              f"{totals['correct'] / totals['n']:.1%}, recall(yes) {rec:.1%}, precision(yes) {prec:.1%}", flush=True)
        batch_df.orderBy(F.desc("p_subscribe")).show(8, truncate=False)      # top leads in this batch
        batch_df.write.mode("append").option("header", True).csv(os.path.join(RESULTS, "part2_predictions"))
        batch_df.unpersist()

    return [scored.writeStream.outputMode("append").foreachBatch(show)
            .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p2").trigger(processingTime="2 seconds").start()]

sections.title: 3. Window Operations and Trend Analysis — 10 s and 1 min windows
sections.answer: With a 30 s watermark, two windowed aggregations run at once: 10-second tumbling windows (count, average balance, % subscribed) and 1-minute sliding windows that move every 20 s (count, average balance). Update mode prints only the windows that changed in each batch; all results are also saved to docs/streaming/part3_*.csv.
sections.code:
def part3(spark, stream):
    banner("PART 3 - Window operations: transaction count and average balance per 10 s and per 1 min window")
    wm = stream.withWatermark("event_time", "30 seconds")
    w10 = (wm.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 seconds"))
           .agg(F.count("*").alias("transactions"), F.round(F.avg("balance"), 1).alias("avg_balance"),
                F.round(100 * F.avg((F.col("y") == "yes").cast("int")), 1).alias("subscribe_pct")))
    w60 = (wm.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "1 minute", "20 seconds"))      # sliding: 1 min long, every 20 s
           .agg(F.count("*").alias("transactions"), F.round(F.avg("balance"), 1).alias("avg_balance")))

    def sink(name):
        def show(batch_df, batch_id):
            if batch_df.isEmpty():
                return
            out = (batch_df.select(F.date_format("window.start", "HH:mm:ss").alias("window_start"),
                                   F.date_format("window.end", "HH:mm:ss").alias("window_end"), "*")
                   .drop("window").orderBy("window_start"))
            print(f"\n----- {name} | micro-batch {batch_id} (windows changed in this batch) -----", flush=True)
            out.show(30, truncate=False)
            out.withColumn("batch_id", F.lit(batch_id)).toPandas().to_csv(
                os.path.join(RESULTS, f"part3_{name.split()[0]}.csv"), mode="a", index=False,
                header=not os.path.exists(os.path.join(RESULTS, f"part3_{name.split()[0]}.csv")))
        return show

    # update mode: only windows that changed are emitted; the watermark lets Spark finalise old windows
    return [w10.writeStream.outputMode("update").foreachBatch(sink("10s tumbling windows"))
            .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p3a").trigger(processingTime="4 seconds").start(),
            w60.writeStream.outputMode("update").foreachBatch(sink("1min sliding windows (slide 20s)"))
            .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p3b").trigger(processingTime="4 seconds").start()]

sections.title: 3. Brief analysis of the trends observed
sections.answer:
• Steady flow: the 28 normal 10-second windows hold 142-151 transactions (median 146), average balance 1,415 ± 265, subscription rate 7-16%.
• Traffic spike: one window carried 429 transactions (about 3x normal). The 1-minute sliding windows covering it rise from about 900 to about 1,170 transactions and fall back after it slides out — a sliding window spreads a spike over 3 windows, a tumbling window isolates it.
• Balance anomalies: two windows had an average balance more than 2 standard deviations above normal (2,000 and 2,272 vs 1,415), caused by a few very rich clients — a live dashboard would flag these.
• Out-of-order data: tiny windows before the first real window (1-6 rows, balances 0 to 4,799) are late events that arrived with old timestamps; they land in the correct historical window, not the current one.
• The final window has only 20 rows because the producer stopped mid-window.

sections.title: 4. Handling Late and Out-of-Order Data — watermarking
sections.answer:
Approach: the same 10-second window count runs twice. WITH withWatermark('event_time', '30 seconds') in append mode, Spark writes each window once, when it is final, and drops rows that arrive more than 30 s after their window closed. WITHOUT a watermark (complete mode) Spark must keep every window in memory forever.
Result: 62 of the 224 late rows were too late and were dropped; the other 162 arrived within the 30 s allowance and were counted in their correct window even though they arrived out of order. Spark kept only 4 windows in state with the watermark versus 35 without. The last windows are 'open' because the watermark had not passed them when the stream ended.
Why it improves accuracy: event-time windows put each transaction where it happened, not where it arrived, so delayed transactions still count in the right time bucket. The watermark is the explicit trade-off — wait up to 30 s for stragglers (accuracy), then close the window to free memory and publish a final number (latency).
sections.code:
def part4(spark, stream):
    banner("PART 4 - Late and out-of-order data: the same 10 s window count WITH and WITHOUT a watermark")
    with_wm = (stream.withWatermark("event_time", "30 seconds")
               .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 seconds")).agg(F.count("*").alias("transactions")))
    no_wm = stream.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 seconds")).agg(F.count("*").alias("transactions"))

    # append mode is only allowed WITH a watermark: a window is written once, when it is final
    final = (with_wm.select(F.date_format("window.start", "HH:mm:ss").alias("window_start"), "transactions")
             .writeStream.outputMode("append").format("memory").queryName("final_windows")
             .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p4a").trigger(processingTime="3 seconds").start())
    # without a watermark Spark must keep every window in state forever (complete mode)
    unbounded = (no_wm.select(F.date_format("window.start", "HH:mm:ss").alias("window_start"), "transactions")
                 .writeStream.outputMode("complete").format("memory").queryName("all_windows")
                 .option("checkpointLocation", f"{CKPT}/p4b").trigger(processingTime="3 seconds").start())
    return [final, unbounded]


def part4_report(spark, queries):
    final, unbounded = queries
    banner("PART 4 - results")
    p = final.lastProgress or {}
    ops = p.get("stateOperators", [{}])
    dropped = sum(o.get("numRowsDroppedByWatermark", 0) for o in ops)
    wm = p.get("eventTime", {}).get("watermark")
    if wm:
        from datetime import datetime, timezone
        wm = datetime.fromisoformat(wm.replace("Z", "+00:00")).astimezone().strftime("%H:%M:%S")
    print("final watermark = max event time seen - 30 s =", wm,
          "-> windows ending before this are final; rows older than this are dropped")
    print("state rows kept   WITH watermark:", sum(o.get("numRowsTotal", 0) for o in ops))
    print("state rows kept WITHOUT watermark:",
          sum(o.get("numRowsTotal", 0) for o in (unbounded.lastProgress or {}).get("stateOperators", [{}])))
    total_dropped = 0
    for q in [final]:
        for prog in q.recentProgress:
            total_dropped += sum(o.get("numRowsDroppedByWatermark", 0) for o in prog.get("stateOperators", []))
    print(f"late rows dropped by the watermark (too late to be counted): {total_dropped} (last batch: {dropped})")
    cmp = spark.sql("""
        SELECT a.window_start, a.transactions AS counted_without_watermark,
               f.transactions AS final_count_with_watermark,
               CASE WHEN f.transactions IS NULL THEN NULL
                    ELSE a.transactions - f.transactions END AS late_rows_dropped,
               CASE WHEN f.transactions IS NULL THEN 'open: watermark has not passed yet'
                    ELSE 'final' END AS status
        FROM all_windows a LEFT JOIN final_windows f USING (window_start)
        ORDER BY a.window_start""")
    cmp.show(60, truncate=False)
    cmp.toPandas().to_csv(os.path.join(RESULTS, "part4_watermark_comparison.csv"), index=False)

sections.title: Partitioning — divide the dataset into partitions for parallel processing
sections.answer: Strategy used: hash partitioning on job into 8 partitions (2 per core). All rows of one job land in the same partition, so groupBy(job) needs no extra shuffle — the plan for round-robin data has an Exchange, the plan for job-partitioned data does not. 8 partitions keep all 4 cores busy. Trade-off: the job key is uneven, so partitions are uneven (round-robin is perfectly balanced but needs a shuffle for every groupBy(job)).

sections.title: Parallel Processing — average balance for each job category
sections.answer: Two parallel approaches with identical results: the DataFrame groupBy (partial aggregate per partition → shuffle → final average) and an explicit RDD map → reduceByKey that combines (sum, count) inside each partition before shuffling. mapPartitionsWithIndex shows exactly which jobs each partition processed.
sections.code:
monitor.mark("avg balance per job")
# (1) DataFrame API: each partition computes partial (sum, count) per job -> shuffle -> final average
t0 = time.time()
avg_df = by_job.groupBy("job").agg(F.round(F.avg("balance"), 2).alias("avg_balance"),
                                   F.count("*").alias("clients")).orderBy(F.desc("avg_balance"))
avg_df.show()
print(f"DataFrame groupBy: {time.time() - t0:.2f}s")

# (2) RDD API, written out explicitly: map -> combine locally per partition -> reduceByKey across partitions
t0 = time.time()
rdd = by_job.select("job", "balance").rdd
partials = rdd.map(lambda r: (r.job, (r.balance, 1)))                      # runs on every partition in parallel
totals = partials.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1]))       # combines inside partitions first
avg_rdd = sorted(((j, round(s / c, 2)) for j, (s, c) in totals.collect()), key=lambda x: -x[1])
print(f"RDD reduceByKey:   {time.time() - t0:.2f}s")
print(avg_rdd)

# Show the work each partition did in parallel (partition id -> jobs and partial sums)
def per_partition(idx, it):
    acc = {}
    for r in it:
        s, c = acc.get(r.job, (0, 0)); acc[r.job] = (s + r.balance, c + 1)
    yield (idx, {k: v[1] for k, v in acc.items()})
for pid, jobs in rdd.mapPartitionsWithIndex(per_partition).collect():
    print(f"partition {pid}: rows per job {jobs}")

sections.title: Parallel Processing — top 5 age groups with the highest loan amounts
sections.answer: Data note: bank.csv has no loan-amount column (housing and loan are yes/no), so loan volume = number of loans (housing + personal) per 5-year age group, plus the total balance of loan holders as a size proxy. Methodology: derive age_group and n_loans per row (every partition works alone), then groupBy does a partial aggregation per partition and one small shuffle. Top group: 30-34 with 807 loans.

from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

cats = ["job", "marital", "education", "default", "housing", "loan", "contact", "month", "poutcome"]
nums = ["age", "balance", "day", "duration", "campaign", "pdays", "previous"]
feat_pipe = Pipeline(stages=[*[StringIndexer(inputCol=c, outputCol=c + "_i", handleInvalid="keep") for c in cats],
                             OneHotEncoder(inputCols=[c + "_i" for c in cats], outputCols=[c + "_o" for c in cats]),
                             VectorAssembler(inputCols=nums + [c + "_o" for c in cats], outputCol="features")])
data = (feat_pipe.fit(df).transform(df.withColumn("label", (F.col("y") == "yes").cast("double")))
        .select("features", "label"))
train, test = data.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)
train = train.repartition(4).cache(); test = test.cache()
print("train partitions:", train.rdd.getNumPartitions(), "| rows per partition:", partition_sizes(train))

sections.title: Model Training — scaling experiment (1 to 32 partitions on 226k rows)
sections.answer: On a 50x copy (226,050 rows), 4 partitions trained 2.1x faster than 1, but 32 partitions was no faster than 1 because tiny tasks add scheduling and aggregation overhead. Challenges and fixes: one input partition (repartition), repeated passes over data (cache), too many partitions (2-3 per core), Python UDFs avoided in hot paths.

sections.title: Resource Monitoring — CPU and memory during processing and training
sections.answer: A background psutil thread samples the Spark JVM every 0.5 s, and Spark's status REST API reports executor memory, tasks and GC time. Observations: Spark averages 2.4-3 cores on small steps and reaches its 4-core limit in the aggregation and scaling phases (short peaks above 4 are JVM garbage-collection/JIT threads); JVM memory grows in steps as data is cached (about 620 MB → 1.44 GB) with the driver capped at 2 GB; GC time (0.3 s) is tiny compared with task time (16 s), so memory is not the bottleneck.

sections.answer: Four independent preprocessing tasks run first one after another, then concurrently from 4 Python threads.
